transcript.title: MICHAEL SALAZAR, Petitioner, v. PARAMOUNT GLOBAL, DBA 247SPORTS, Respondent

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: We will hear argument this morning in Case 25-459, Salazar versus Paramount Global.  Mr. Hammack.

Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Outraged by the disclosure of one person's video-watching history, Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act.  In Section (b)(1), the Act provides for civil  liability when a video tape service provider knowingly discloses personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider.  The Act defines three of those terms. At bottom, a video tape service provider is the kind of entity that will owe obligations under the law.  Personally identifiable information  is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E).  And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1).  The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years.  Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent.  These are not one -off disclosures.  They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone,  including a consumer, watches a video on the website.  Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures.  All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get.  Paramount just  didn't get it.  So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer."  But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable  information," not in the definition of "consumer."  That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But wouldn't it be natural to think that goods or services from a video tape service provider would be video-related services?

Not at all, Justice Thomas, because, here, we have material variations at every stage of the statute, at every stage of the definitions section.  So we  start with a "video tape service provider." That definition refers to prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.  That's one subject matter.  In (a)(3)'s definition of "personally identifiable information," we have video  -- video materials or services.  That's a second subject matter that's different in scope from  (a)(4)'s definition of a provider.  And then, in (a)(1), the "consumer" definition, we have goods or services.  And all three subject matters are coming from a video tape service provider. That they're different tells us that a provider can do all three things.  It can engage in  transactions concerning all three.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, our former colleague, Justice Breyer, confronted with questions like this, you know, his  favorite hypothetical in that area anyway was a sign in a park that says, you know, no pets in  the park, and the question was, did that mean that the person carrying his pet snail in his pocket was subject to prosecution.  I mean, don't we have to look at the general purpose that's involved here before determining that the statute reaches as far as you would have it?

I think we are completely in line with the statutory purpose. And we have no objection, of course, to the Court looking to that purpose.  And I don't  mean "purpose" in the sense of scouring the legislative history, but look at the text of Section (b)(1), which specifically prohibits the disclosure of personally identifiable  information concerning any consumer.  We have two different limitations within that section.  "Personally identifiable information" is one limitation.  "Concerning  any consumer" is a second.  And the reading, I think the appropriate reading, of those two things together, which exist in (b)(1) but not in other sections of the VPPA, which protect against  -- for example, in subsection (D), we've got the admissibility provision. Personally identifiable information won't be  admissible unless it's obtained in compliance with the VPPA.  In subsection (E), we've got personally identifiable information, an affirmative requirement that providers destroy personally identifiable information after a period of time.  In neither location is that personally identifiable information linked to a consumer. It's only in (b)(1) that that link happens, so we know that (b)(1) is protecting less personally identifiable information from disclosure, not more.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Hammack, is it your position  --I'm thinking about the limits. Is it your position that any company that has a short up on its website, be it a commercial or whatever, is a video service provider?

That's not our position, Justice Barrett.  And I would say the -- the definition of "video tape service provider" in (a)(4), which, by the way, isn't at issue here,  is very clear that you have to be engaged in the business of renting, selling, or delivering those audiovisual materials.  So it's not  everyone who happens to deliver them.  It's not everyone who provides a video once.  You have to be engaged in that business.  And that's  another real limitation on liability in (b)(1).

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Is your theory that 247Sports was in engaged in that business or that Paramount was?
Well, in this case, Paramount Global is doing business as --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: As.  Okay.
--247Sports.  So I think both is the answer.  But, yes, our  position is absolutely that Paramount Global is a video tape service provider.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So you -- Mr. Clement used in his brief some examples, of Chick-fil-A, et cetera.  Would you take the position that if Chick -fil -A had some videos on its website, it's a video tape service provider?

We would not take that position.  And it should come as no surprise  that the court that confronted that particular problem found that Chick-fil-A is not a video tape service provider.  That's how the motion to dismiss was granted in that case.  We have no quarrel with that holding.  We don't find it particularly surprising.  But that's nothing  like what Paramount Global does here.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If Congress's interest was the protection of privacy of a person's video tape watching, why would the disclosure of personally identifiable  information be limited only to consumers and not to those who watch videos for free?

Well, I guess I want to be very clear because the person who watches videos for free can still be protected by  (b)(1)'s disclosure prohibition as long as he's a consumer of something else from that provider.  He's rented, purchased, or subscribed to some  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But the provider has to be in the business of -- but --so why wouldn't Congress just protect at large anyone who's watching videos, free or not free?

I would say I think there are several kind of overlapping reasons  that Congress might have preferred the exact regime it enacted.  I think the clearest one is that the consumer relationship provides an easy window for getting consent, and Congress was very concerned about consent and the  -- the consumer controlling the disclosure of personally identifiable information.  So having that window to get consent and, if you look at the 2013 amendments, you've got consent even for a two -year window.  So advance consent comes into play.  That consumer  window is very important in terms of identifying the place to get consent.  It could also be that Congress just thought this regime was more fair.  You've got a consumer that's exchanged something of value with the provider, and, therefore, they're entitled to the protections and the possibility of liquidated damages.  But whatever we  --I don't  -- I won't dispute that there is some mystery about why Congress did something different in (b)(1) than it did in, for example, Sections (d) and (e)  when it protected personally identifiable information there.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Can you explain exactly how the consent would work in your opinion?

Absolutely.  So consent works by allowing a provider to disclose personally identifiable information, and there are several locations where a provider can get that consent.  One is the initiation of the consumer transaction.  Another is when the  person watches a video, you could have a banner pop up and --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: A non-video consumer transaction you're talking about there, right?

It could be a non-video consumer transaction, or it could be a video consumer transaction.  I think the statute is indifferent as to those two possibilities.  Or  it could be that the provider gets consent just simply before the disclosure is made.  I think, again, the statute is indifferent as to when the provider obtains that consent so long as it gets it before the disclosure is made.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Could it be also that  --I'm going back to Justice Sotomayor's question  -- that we have a statute that was enacted at a time in which it wasn't really conceivable that you could access videos without purchasing them or renting them?  In other words, I'm just wondering whether we have sort of limitations in the facts that we need to think about a little bit in  -- in -- in trying to assess what Congress's intent was here?

I -- I'm not sure it's true that in 1988 it was inconceivable that someone might watch a video on a computer.  I think Congress was very concerned with the  changing technological advances and -- and computer technology.  But even more in 2013, when Congress stepped back into this statute and revised just the consent provision, I think it was intimately aware -- and, again, this is in the legislative history  --it was intimately aware with the fact that people were streaming all sorts of videos to their phones and to their  computers all the time.  And I think it's important to note both personally identifiable information in (a)(3) and the consumer relationship in (a)(1) are technology-neutral.  Requested or obtained doesn't identify any technology by which you'll request or obtain videos.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But I guess I'm just trying to go back maybe to even Justice Thomas's first question, which is, what is your theory as to why Congress has a broader category of consumers than the personally identified information and video tape service provider categories?

Well, I think the  -- the  --the definitions are different.  We know that for sure because, if you just line them up and look at them, there are a number of material variations between them.  As to why they're different  -- and this goes back to the point I was trying to make earlier  -- there might be some mystery about why they're different.  Whether they're different is very clear.  And I think we just have to live with that mystery a little bit rather than rewrite the statute.  But, again, I think there are good reasons and -- and, in fact, it might close  loopholes to have them do different work because a business could structure its relationship with individuals so that you never rent, purchase, or subscribe directly to the  video materials.  You request or obtain them  some other way.  And you rent, purchase, or subscribe to something else entirely.  Congress wrote this statute so that that sort of clever structure by a provider won't create a loophole that allows a  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, I mean, I thought your answer was going to be something like, really, the point of this statute was Congress's concern.  You started with the  concern about the release of video-watching history as it relates to one person.  And so, really, the consumer, who is the consumer is not the thrust of this.  The thrust of this is the video tape service  provider and their activity with respect to releasing or disclosing this information.  And Congress wanted to  --or maybe -- maybe wanted to have the consumer relationship for the purposes that you indicated earlier, like consent or whatnot.  But, for some of us, it matters why.  And  --and mysteries aren't great.  So I'm trying to come up with or understand the theory that Congress would have  crafted a statute in this way.

So I'm not sure I could have said it any better myself.  I think you're absolutely right to be focused on the thrust of this statute is about personally identifiable information.  Every operative provision of this  statute protects some amount of personally identifiable information; (b)(1) just has another limitation so that it protects not all personally identifiable information but just the personally identifiable information concerning a consumer.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Hammack, speaking of personally -- personally identiful  --identifiable information  -- sorry -- that definition uses "includes" instead of "means."  Does it sweep more broadly than the definition given there?  What else could be in it?  Why  -- why would it say just "includes"?  What else does it --

So the parties agree that "personally identifiable information,"  although it says "includes," requires two strands of information:  Something that identifies you and something that identifies  the specific video materials or services that you requested or obtained.  All the courts of appeals that have addressed that question have reached the exact same conclusion.  If you look at the legislative history, Congress actually says why  it used the word "includes" instead of "means."  And it says we used "includes" there to create a floor, to create a minimum. Personally identifiable information could identify you or  --or identify facts about you in lots of other realms, but, at a minimum, it has to identify you as having requested or obtained those specific video --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Personally  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And so that's a limit -- oh, sorry.  Go ahead.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Go ahead, please.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So go ahead.  I'm done.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, I was just going to ask:  Personally identifiable by whom?  By  the NSA?  I mean, how specific does this have to be?

I think the answer to that question lies in subsection (b)(1), the  liability provision, which says it prohibits disclosures of PII to any person.  So, if it's identifiable to the "any person" that receives that disclosure, it's personally identifiable information.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You -- you said before that "includes" was used to suggest a floor, which makes perfect sense.  But I think that the question is, does "includes" -- does that  provision with the word "includes" also have a ceiling?  I think that that's the question that would give rise to some concern.  If you  thought "includes" could also mean anything else in the world, then you wouldn't have the limit that you're saying comes from that provision.

I think, if you can imagine a disclosure that includes 10 different facts about an individual and just one of them identifies the specific video materials or  services that he requested or obtained, Congress is saying that disclosure of that information is personally identifiable  information only because of that one strand of information.  It might have identified --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I see.  But that one strand has to be there?
Absolutely, yes, yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And the question of PII, even if you prevail on the issue before us, would still be resolved on remand, correct?
That's correct.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It would still be open on remand?  We're not resolving that here because there's a big argument, obviously, in the courts of appeals whether this kind of  information constitutes PII, correct?
That is correct.  And this Court may someday have to resolve that question, but that day is not today.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Is that why you asked us  -- is --is that -- is that why you asked us to vacate instead of remand?
That  --that's exactly why.  There are other arguments that  -- that Paramount raised below, and that's why we asked to vacate.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: In  --including whether it's a video tape service provider?
In the district court, it raised that question, not in the Sixth Circuit.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Not in the Sixth Circuit?  But it is claiming that these videos  are for free and not part of a consumer transaction, correct?

Well, it's certainly claiming that the videos are available for free.  And our response is, sure, they're delivered for free and you might request or obtain them for free, but that doesn't change  the operative provisions of the statute either in  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No.  But then would they be in the  --in the business of -- of  -- of in commerce for rental, sale, or delivery?  That's up to the lower courts, correct?
I -- I think that's exactly right.  Our position is yes, but that's a question for remand.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How have these suits generally prevailed in the lower courts?
I'm sorry, what -- what do you mean by "prevailed"?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Have the plaintiffs won?
I think, if you look at Paramount's brief, it suggests that courts have  routinely dismissed VPPA claims.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And why do you think that is?  Why do you think these smart lower  court judges have rejected the kind of very literal interpretation of the statutory  language that you're presenting to us today?
I -- I think there's --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Under every provision of this  -- of this statute, why -- why have they rejected that?

I think there is, unfortunately, some reluctance to -- to believe  that Congress actually meant what it said in the context of this statute.  It wrote a broad  law that is very protective of personally identifiable information.  That prohibits a lot of disclosures of that kind of information, and I think  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, it enacted a law that is based on the technology of the 1980s.  And you can see this in every provision of this, in the title, Wrongful Disclosure of Video Tape Rental or Sale -- or Sale Records.  And you can go through all the provisions, and it's like that.  Suppose we look at (a)(1) and don't consider the statutory definition of "video tape service provider."  Is Paramount a video tape service provider in the literal sense of the  -- of the term?
Yes, it is.  And, in fact  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: In the literal sense of the term?  Are they selling video tapes, VHS tapes?
It -- it's very important there that in (a)(4), the definition of "video tape service provider," it says "or similar audiovisual materials."

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.  Okay.  That's what I'm saying.  But, if we go to that, what does it  --what does its  --what does it mean for it to be similar?

Again, it's not a question that's presented here, but you have, I think, several avenues.  One way is to say it's similar in that it's prerecorded.  It's similar  in that you watch it in the privacy of your home.  It's similar in that it can be delivered to you personally; it's not something that you, for example, go to a theater and witness with other people.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But it is not similar in the sense that you go to a Blockbuster store and get a VHS tape.

Which is true enough, I guess, and, in fact, when Congress stepped back  into the statute in 2013, it acknowledged that video cassette tapes were largely obsolete, Blockbuster was either on its way out or  already gone, and everyone was streaming videos directly to their phones.  Congress saw no need to re-jigger the definitions or to change the provisions at (b)(1)(D) or (E) precisely because they're technology -neutral.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, isn't there a concern about repurposing a statute that was  really about public disclosure of what individuals viewed into a statute that regulates data sharing for targeted advertising on the Internet?  Those are very different things.  And the context here is the data sharing for the targeted advertising.

So, on the first point, I would say, again, Congress wrote a law that isn't technology -specific.  It wrote a broad law that spans all kinds of technologies, all kinds of ways that you might obtain those video materials or services, all kinds of ways you might rent, purchase, or subscribe to goods or services.  And then the second point, Congress anticipated that this information would be useful for advertising purposes, and it crafted  an exception under (b)(2)(D) that specifically allows disclosures of the subject matter of the videos, along with a name and address, when that disclosure is made exclusively or solely  for the purpose of advertising goods or services directly to the consumer.  And it's important there goods or service  -- it says "goods and services" in (b)(2)(D)(ii), that  --that exception, and it says "goods or services" in subsection (a)'s definition of "consumer."  Our reading has "goods or services" and "goods and services" mean the same thing. By its own admission, Paramount's reading has those two virtually identical phrases mean two radically different things.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You're  --you're hypothesizing a prescient Congress, as opposed to a Congress that mistakenly stumbled into  broader language than it meant to use.

I think that is kind of the foundational premise that this Court indulges at the outset of every statutory interpret  --or interpretation case, namely, that Congress said what it meant and meant what it said when it wrote a statute.  I think, if you start from the opposite purpose, that maybe Congress accidentally kind of tripped and fell and wrote these words instead of those words, I think, if you indulge that premise, you actually end up landing in the exact same place precisely  because, when you walk through (a)(4)'s definition of a "provider," (a)(3)'s definition  of "PII," and then (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer," you see that these weren't accidental.  The scopes are different every  time even though the source is the same.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Hammack, I want to ask you about standing.  So the Sixth  Circuit recognized in a footnote that its view of standing here, saying that this was similar to publicity given private life, diverged from the Eleventh Circuit's approach to the question.  And I want you to give me the pitch on the facts of your complaint as you allege them why you have standing and specifically here,  you know, you can have disputes about, as the Eleventh Circuit has taken the position, that you need to have some publicity, telling one private individual isn't enough, but, here, so far as I can tell, no person got this information, whatever this pixel thing is, right?  So why do you have standing?

Well, the person, I suppose, would be Facebook that got the information, just the largest social media  company that exists.  But it's also true -- and I think, if you -- if you look closely at the Sixth Circuit's opinion, it actually says all  six circuits that have answered that standing question in the context of a VPPA claim are in accord.  All of them say, yes, you have  standing when there's been a disclosure even to one person of your personally identifiable  information without your consent.  All six are in accord on that point.  The difference with the Eleventh Circuit is, well, what happens in a different context.  I believe that was the FDCPA instead of the VPPA.  But, in that context, you  basically bounced a disclosure from a mail vendor to the consumer, and the court said in that context that's not really a disclosure. You're basically outsourcing kind of who's going to mail the item to the consumer.  Here, we've got an exception for disclosures made to the consumer.  It's an open question, I guess, whether a similar mail vendor theory would apply to the VPPA, but  that's just radically different than the facts we have here.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You all didn't brief standing, right?  Is that an issue in this case  right now?
It --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean, it always is in the sense of our jurisdiction, but I'm just saying, do we have arguments written related to  -- to standing?

That's actually -- that  --that's absolutely right, that it was not put up in issue in this case.  We argued that in the district court.  Paramount  abandoned its standing argument in the Sixth Circuit.  It addressed it sua sponte.  I think  you're right that it's a background issue in this case.  But it has not been briefed.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And can I ask you a clarifying question just about the lower court dismissals?  I -- are they on the consumer issue that is before us now?  I thought there was a 2-2 split among the circuits on the definition of "consumer."

That's absolutely right. There is a 2-2 split on the definition of "consumer."  And both dismissals here, the -- the district court in Tennessee and the Sixth Circuit, held solely that this complaint should be dismissed because of the particular meaning we're giving to the word "consumer."

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So, if these have not prevailed in large, it could be for other reasons than that?
Absolutely.  And, in fact  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.

-- it often is for other reasons.  If you look at Paramount's brief in opposition to our petition for certiorari, they point to personally identifiable information,  disputes about whether someone is a provider. Those are other reasons, and they point to the  fact that there are multiple real limitations to liability coexisting at once in subsection (b)(1).

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Is  --the PII, is that a 3-1 split against your position on PII?
That  --that's correct, Your Honor, yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I think the other side's kind of big-picture argument is that we are a textualist Court but usually not a literalist Court and that we have a lot of principles and doctrines  --major questions, elephants in mouse holes, context, common sense -- you see those terms sprinkled through a lot of our cases, including in this general field, and that we should be thinking about  that so that we don't read this statute for all it's worth when the Congress in the 1980s wasn't thinking about data sharing for targeted advertising.  So that's a big-picture question for you to tackle.

I think this Court's approach is exactly right, that you always look at text in context.  We have no quarrel with that methodology because text in context shows  you exactly what you normally presume at the outset, which is that Congress meant "goods or services," a broader term, when it said "goods or services" in subsection (a)(1).  It did not mean video materials or services, something it said in the same sentence, identically from a video tape service provider.  It did not mean prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.  It didn't even mention services at  all in the definition, (a)(4)'s definition, of a "provider."  It didn't mean those other phrases that it said elsewhere.  It meant something different.  And I think context absolutely reinforces that point.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, Mr. Clement says your client is not  --was not a consumer  -- was not a subscriber of services from a video tape service provider because what he subscribed to was a newsletter.  So would you address that?  He says that the "from" places a limitation on the literal  -- what might be considered the literal interpretation of those phrases, and he has  lots of examples in -- in which "from" is used in that way.

I think that's an unusual meaning to ascribe to "from" from the outset.  That is usually a word that identifies  the source of material, not something that identifies the scope.  And, here, we know for sure that Congress was looking at "from" as identifying source.  And we know that by comparing (a)(1)'s  definition of "consumer" to (a)(3)'s definition of "PII."  Both identify subject matter that comes from a video tape service provider.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean, there are a lot of examples in which "from" is used in exactly the way Mr. Clement tells us, and I -- I don't have to add an additional hypothetical, but I will anyway.  Let's say I  --I got gas at a Costco or a Sam's Club, and then I'm having a  conversation with my neighbor, who's complaining about the high cost of gas, and he says:  I had to pay X per gallon -- Chief?  All right.  I had to pay X per gallon for gas. And I said:  Well, I paid X minus 20 cents.  And he says:  Wow.  Where did you get your gas?  And I say:  I got it from a provider of optical services because Sam's Club and Costco have optical services as well.  Now would  --would I be -- I would just be playing games if I said that, wouldn't I?

I think, in that specific context, that would be a pretty unusual thing to say.  But, if we could twist it just a little bit, it would be equally odd  to say if we had a statute that defined gas stations a particular way, those that provide fuel, that would be our (a)(4) paradigm.  Then we had in the same statute, the same sentence of the same statute, a provision that mentioned fuel materials or services or fuel goods or services.  That's (a)(3).  And  then we had in the same statute, the same sentence, goods or services from a gas station.  It would be exceedingly odd to say those three subject matters must be the same thing.  Maybe I was feeling really brave at the gas station and I got sushi.  That's a good or service from  -- (Laughter.)
-- a gas station, but it's not a fuel good or service, and it's certainly not the fuel that you would normally buy at a gas station.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  Justice Thomas, anything further?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The -- I'd like you to go back to your definition of a "video tape service provider."  It means "any person"  -- I'm just reading from the statute -- "any person engaged in the business in or affecting interstate commerce of rental" -- "rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials."  How does that get us to streaming, to video that is streamed?

I think the courts  --as far as I know at least, the courts are in accord that "or similar audiovisual materials" includes things like streaming videos to a personal device that you would watch in your house.  It doesn't require a physicality, you know, necessarily that you're going to have a  tape, a physical tape that you play that way.  And, again, when you look at, in 2013, Congress stepped back into this statute, it specifically said, we are aware streaming is  rampant and we still think this statute covers the  --the personally identifiable information that results from those streaming activities.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How, in your own words, though, does that similar audiovisual  material get you to streamed video?

Because it's similar in critical ways to a video cassette tape.  It allows you to watch that video in the privacy of your home.  It allows you to watch it on your own.  It allows you to pause, come back later, record  --or, I'm sorry, rewind, and pick it up as you wish.  It's -- it's in lots  of ways the exact same as the way you would interact with a video cassette tape.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Why isn't that closer to, during the 1980s, you had cassette tapes,  you had the Blockbuster, you -- you rented the cassette tapes, the VHS, but you also had TV and you had cable?  Wouldn't it seem that  streaming is closer to cable TV than it is to picking up a video from Blockbuster?

If we're looking at the technology that was available in 1988, I think  the answer has to be no precisely because you couldn't pause and rewind and stop and come  back hours later and rewatch things the way that you can now both with a prerecorded video cassette tape and with the exact audiovisual materials that we have at issue here.  And I would note too all of this concerns whether Paramount is a video tape  service provider, which isn't before the Court today.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor? Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch? Justice Kavanaugh?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Just on the video tape service provider issue, I know that's not before us, but I think you've waved away some  of the concerns about every business in America that has video on its website being targeted.  But, certainly, the amicus briefs on the other side -- The Retail Litigation Center, the Chamber of Commerce  -- point out that your reading would  --and  --and suits have been brought against every sector of the economy -- print media publishers, movie theaters, advocacy groups, sports leagues, health and fitness websites, parenting advice companies, chess websites, crafting websites, professional networking sites, universities -- every other  type of defendant under the sun in the words of the amicus brief.  And so I think you've waved away some of the concerns about the breadth of your  argument on this issue by saying, don't worry, it's not going to apply because of the definition of "video tape service provider."  But I don't think other plaintiffs are going to be conceding that in the cases against  those businesses, or is the amicus -- are the amicus briefs wrong in saying that that's a legitimate concern?

Well, I would say a couple of points.  One, it's true that those suits have been brought.  It's also true that  many of them have resulted in district courts saying:  Wait a minute, that entity, like Chick-fil-A, is not a video tape service provider.  This is the wrong kind of entity. Congress wasn't targeting Chick-fil-A.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And what makes someone a video tape service provider?  If they have a video on their business website that, let's say, is three minutes long, are they a video tape service provider?

I'm not sure the length of the video matters.  What will always matter is exactly what (a)(4) says.  You have to be  engaged in the business of renting, selling, or delivering that audiovisual material.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You're delivering it, right, by showing it on your website, correct?
That  --that seems to me to be true.  You're delivering it.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  And then what makes you --
But are you engaged --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- what makes you in the business?  Two minutes, three minutes, four minutes, 10 minutes?  What is it?
I don't think the number of minutes long that a video is.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What does matter then?
I think it's  -- it's exactly what Congress put into (a)(4).  Are you engaged in that business?  Chick-fil-A is not.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I'm trying to -- I'm trying to  --
Paramount is.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I understand the words that are used.  And I don't mean to be  too sharp, but I just want to have some explanation of what you think "engaged in the  business" means because I think you waved away some of the concerns by saying, don't worry about Chick -fil -A, and I just want to know why.

Well, I think, if you  -- if you imagine the Blockbuster paradigm, it was engaged in the business of delivering those  materials because that was what was on offer when you walked into the store.  The same is true of a department store.  When you walked in those doors, you could rent, purchase -- rent or purchase at least those --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: When you go on a business's website, which is how a lot of  people shop, obviously, most people, you'll often see a video quickly and --

And  -- and it might -- it  -- it might be that those websites are in the business of delivering those video materials.  I don't think that should alarm us so much precisely because (b)(1) has multiple other limitations in it.  You also need PII to be collected. You need a knowing disclosure, not an accidental one, a knowing disclosure.  You also need a consumer.  So I think, even if we lived in a world where, for example, Chick-fil-A someday becomes a video tape service provider, there  are lots of other off-ramps for liability included.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I still don't think you've told me what a video -- and this  is the last time I'm going to ask it -- what on the business's website's video makes it in the business of delivering?

I apologize, Justice Kavanaugh, I'm not sure I have a better answer  except to say putting that material on offer in your store, you are driving  -- your -- your profit or your business motive is linked to renting, selling, or delivering that material.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: A video of your product presumably.  Okay, thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Barrett?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And why do you allege that 247Sports meets that description?
Precisely because it is engaged in the business of delivering a whole host of video materials on its website.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, that's just sort of repeating back the definition.  But what makes it a provider?  You say it's engaged in the business.  Why?  And what -- you know, what is the length of these videos?  Why  -- why are they similar to the old, you know, VHS tape?

Again, I'm not sure that they're similar in terms of length, but, again, it's the profit motive that Paramount has when it makes these deliveries.  It doesn't deliver them, you know, for kicks.  It delivers them because it sells advertising.  It drives business to the website.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, that's back to Justice Kavanaugh's concern because that's why every video -- I mean, if I'm on Nordstrom's website and I click to -- to see the model show me what the shoes are going to look like, the mode  --that's a profit motive.  It's not doing it just for kicks, I mean, so that does bring in things like Chick-fil-A and basically every other business.

I think the courts have been very consistent in saying it doesn't bring in every kind of business that incidentally happens to provide a single video on its website.  That's certainly not our position either.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Jackson?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So, even if we someday define the universe of video tape service providers because that's not in this  case, but even if we define it broadly, can you speak to whether interpreting "consumer" as you  have will have the negative consequences?  There's a lot of policy arguments in Respondent's brief, and I just wanted to invite you to talk about what the cure for this would be even if this is a broadly interpreted statute.

I don't think it has any real negative consequence here precisely  because all of the elements in (b)(1) have to coexist at the same time, so it's not just that  you're a video tape service provider and, certainly, that this statute does not prohibit providers from having consumers.  It doesn't  prohibit them even from collecting or using personally identifiable information.  The only thing that triggers liability, the only thing is the disclosure,  the knowing disclosure, of personally identifiable information concerning a consumer without consent.  And, again, consent is easy to obtain.  That's the easiest off-ramp to liability that we have.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So that's  --so the cure is pretty simple.  It's not that we have  to worry so much about roping in all of these businesses.  They would just figure out a way to get consent from people who are watching these videos after they've been disclosed?

Absolutely true.  And I would say it's -- it's kind of a technological reality that more businesses are engaged in this business today than were engaged in it in 1988, and that's not a concern for exactly the reasons we just laid out:  Consent is such an easy fix.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.
Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  Mr. Clement.

Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  In 1988, Congress addressed a specific problem with a tailored solution, protecting the personally identifiable information of  consumers of video tape service providers.  For years, the statute worked as designed.  Personal protection of video -- information of video consumers was protected, and there was  virtually no litigation under this statute. Then, however, the plaintiffs' class action bar discovered the VPPA and its  statutory and punitive damages.  The key to their effort to repurpose the statute is the argument, the claim, that the statute's definition of "consumer" uses the phrase "goods  or services" in an unmodified way, so one can become a consumer without ever having rented, purchased, or subscribed to a video.  That argument fails at the threshold because the phrase "goods or services" is not unmodified in the statute, but it takes its meaning from the immediate surrounding text. And that immediately surrounding text makes clear that the relevant goods or services are the prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar  audiovisual materials that one could rent, purchase, subscribe to, from a video tape service provider.  So just as one, when referring to goods or services from a medical service provider, would not logically refer to a cup of  coffee or valet parking, when one refers to goods or services from a video tape service provider, one does not logically refer to chicken sandwiches or dog bandanas.  The alternative of interpreting the statute to create a veritable army of VPPA consumers without any personal information to  protect unless and until years or even decades later they watch a free video has nothing to  recommend it and underscores that Petitioner is misreading the statute.  I welcome the Court's questions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Would you tell me how is  -- is -- and I thought it was 247Sports, but 247Sports  --I always thought of it as simply a sports site.  The -- how does it convert to or is seen now by Petitioner as a video tape service provider?  What's the logic of that?  Because,  if its primary business is simply sports and it shows videos, it would seem just naturally not to be a  -- in the business of providing video service.

So, Justice Thomas, with all due respect to my friend, I think he gets there the exact same way you would get there in understanding that Chick-fil-A is in the business of delivering videos.  It's the same thing.  That's not what the website is mostly about, but there -- if you go to the website,  the first thing you'll see is, like, a video starts playing.  You don't even have to click on anything.  It just starts playing.  And that's the way that most websites work these days.  And -- and most of the websites also have pixels because most of the reason you can  get to free content, rather than being behind the pay wall, is because of targeted --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Does that mean they're in the business, though, of delivering video services?
So, I mean, look --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: They're in the business  --Chick -fil-A is in the business of selling chicken sandwiches.  Twenty  -- 247Sports is a sports site that has videos.

Totally agree with you, Justice Thomas, as a common-sense matter.  But here is I think a little bit of the problem, which is Congress did make it pretty clear that the department store, when it sells the video, is a video tape service provider even though, when it sells furniture and clothes and everything else, it's not a video tape service provider.  And the way I think, you know, I would -- the way I understand my friend's  position is, yeah, it's all well and good that 247Sports.com is mostly just a sports site, but, because there are videos on it, that's enough to get you in the business of delivering videos.  And that's the same way the plaintiffs -- they might not have succeeded, but that's the same way the plaintiffs got to Chick-fil-A, La -Z-Boy, Folger's, Godiva chocolates, and, of course, every newspaper virtually, you know, lots of small newspapers, because all of those newspapers, you know,  they're basically in the business of having websites that have news.  Some of the news articles are accompanied by videos.  And, of course, their theory is not that you become a consumer just by going to the website.  That's kind of the weird thing about  this theory.  Their theory when they sue the newspapers is, well, not everybody that goes there is a consumer, but the people that actually still subscribe to the good old-fashioned paper that comes to your door, they are consumers because they bought a non-video or they subscribed to a non-video product.  That gets them in the consumer door. And then maybe five years later, they go to the website  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, Mr. Clement  --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well  --
-- and see a video, and all of a sudden we're off to the races.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- you've picked some hypotheticals that are particularly helpful for you.  Chick-fil-A, you don't think of that as anything other than chicken.  But there are a lot of stores that sell a lot of different things, including the type of videos that we're talking about.  And  so I don't know why we should focus just on the easy hypotheticals.
Well, it's sort of my job to focus on the easy hypotheticals.  (Laughter.)
But I think, if you --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I would think your job is to focus on the hard ones -- (Laughter.)

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- at least from our point of view.

Well, my  --my  --my job is to direct your attention to the easy hypotheticals, I would suppose.  But, fair  enough, your job is to direct to the harder hypotheticals.  But I'm not sure there really are that many hard hypotheticals in the sense that we're not taking the position that if you do -- actually are in the business, you are a video tape service provider, that because you do lots of other things or the -- or the rest, that you're not covered.  And we think -- I mean, you know, I think we would take the position, though I think Justice Thomas raises a good question about streaming services, but we would take the  position that Netflix, when you go online to Netflix, that that might still be covered.  So I think the core of the -- of the statute is still covered under our view. But what I think what we would say is that this notion that you can just mix -- mix and match what makes you a consumer and what gives you the personally identifiable  information that the statute protects for consumers, that mismatch doesn't make any sense.  So a dog bandana  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I don't know if it's mixing and matching.  It's following the  definitions where they lead.  So this definition says "goods and services."  It  doesn't say "audiovisual goods and services." Other definitions do have the modifier in them.  That suggests that the fact that this definition does not have the modifier in it is especially important.  And you  -- you -- you can't get the modifier from the "from" clause because the "from" clause just tells you what -- where you're getting the goods and services from, but the goods and services are the goods and services not modified in any other way.  So mixing and matching, there are three different definitions.  You have to put them together.  What you get, most naturally read, is the Petitioner's understanding of the statute.

Well, two things, Your Honor.  I mean, one, you know, sometimes when  that's what you get, maybe you should take another look.  And the premise of your question, of course, is that "from a video tape service provider" isn't doing any definitional work in the definition of "consumer."  And I would just take issue with that. I mean, you know, "from a video tape service provider," "video tape service provider" is a defined term in the statute.  If you plug that definition into the statute, then what you get  is "consumer" means any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from any person engaged in the business in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.  After I'm done plugging that into the statute, I'm left with the conclusion that the goods or service we're talking about here are prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But they don't have to be, Mr. --
That makes sense --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But they  --but they don't have to be.  I mean, we -- we talked about hypotheticals.  Let me -- let me give you  what I hope is a hard hypothetical that you can address.  So suppose we had Justice Breyer  --he was mentioned before  --entering a video store, and the store not only rents and sells videos but also books about films.  And Justice Breyer is particularly interested in foreign films, so he buys a book at the counter about French  films.  And as he's flipping through the book, he sees mention of several films that he would actually like to preview in the store before he decides whether he wants to rent or buy them. And they have that service.  And he says:  Can  I please go into the corner here, to the machine, and watch X, Y, Z film?  So he does this.  A reporter then comes in and acquires his video-watching history as a result of this escapade, and he has not actually purchased the films.  He's only purchased the book, but he's in the video store and he's watching the films, and his  history then gets disclosed to the reporter.  What I can't figure out is why it would matter from Congress's standpoint that he's only purchased a book under those  circumstances when, really, what Congress cared about is whether his video -watching history was disclosed to a third party under this statute.

So I guess what I would say is that, you know, no statute pursues its purpose to the ends of the earth.  And, here,  Congress was very clear that if you don't have a rental, purchaser, or subscription relationship, then you're not covered by this statute.  And that's common ground between both parties.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right.  He has a purchaser relationship.  What he's purchased is  a good of the video store that is not a film or audiovisual.  He's purchased a book that the video store sells, so he is a consumer of the video store.  Your position, as I take it, would be that because he has not purchased video materials, he's not a consumer for the purpose  of this statute, and I'm asking you why that is.

That's because of the way the statute's written.  And for those that look at legislative history, that also seems entirely consistent with what Congress said.  Congress envisioned the possibility of a department store selling videos and other things, and they were quite clear that they didn't think there was privacy protection for the other things.  And then I also  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But privacy protection for the other things.  So, if the  reporter had asked what book did he buy, then that's not covered.  But the reporter asked  what videos did he watch, and that seems to me to be materially indistinguishable from the actual scenario that gave rise to this statute.

But, with respect, I think, if Justice Breyer went into the same store, didn't buy the book but still looked at three videos in some cabin and didn't have to  subscribe anything to do it, and the reporter asked the same question, he would still fit --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: He doesn't cover the  --
--he would  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- he doesn't cover the  -- the consumer definition on its face because he's not a consumer.  He hasn't  purchased any goods or services.

Right, right.  But it's a perfect illustration of how the statute doesn't capture every disclosure of personal identifying information.  It requires you to be a consumer.  And, logically, the transaction that makes you a consumer is one that involves some personal identifying information.  And what's  illogical is that you become a consumer on day one, and then there's personal identifiable information doesn't catch up to you --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What -- what seems --
-- until day -- until years later.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What seems different to me about now from the 1980s is not so much the -- the plaintiffs but the type of personal identifying information.  It's not your name being released.  It's this data-sharing code, right?  And that's quite a bit different.  And there are a lot of arguments about PII.  And then treating everyone as a video tape service provider, every business as opposed to the ones that are analogous to  Blockbuster.  But those two arguments, both of which may be raised in future cases in which your side's prevailing in the lower courts for  the most part, are not the issues before us.  So how do we think about, you know, the sky-is-falling concern in the amicus briefs and it's part of your brief when there are these two other arguments that you may prevail on?  And why shouldn't we just follow "consumer" as written and worry about that in a future case?

So a couple of things, Justice Kavanaugh.  I mean, first of all, like, if you're going to tell me that I'm going to win on those other arguments, I mean, great.  But we don't know that.  My friend has  -- you know, thinks that he has great arguments on both PII and on video tape service provider.  I also don't think you can really  get away from the definition of "video tape service provider" in interpreting the scope of "consumer" because that word, that defined  word, is part of the definition of "consumer."  But I also want to say there are distinct problems with this expansive definition of "consumer," and it really takes  you away from the structure of the statute because this statute operates on the assumption that consumers are going to have personally  identifiable information and they are going to be the ones -- the consumers are going to be in  the position to consent to the disclosure of that information.  And my friend's position breaks that structure of the statute because, even when he answers Justice Jackson and says the way this is going to work is we're going to ask for consent from everybody before they go for a website, well, they are going to ask for  consent from everybody and they're going to ask for consent from a whole bunch of people who aren't consumers.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, it's going to be overbroad consent, no doubt.  But you  -- it's a very easy solution for these businesses going forward.  And I get the retrospective liability, believe me.  But going forward, it's a very easy solution to get consent, isn't it?  That's a question.  And maybe it's not easy.  But --
So I'd like  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- tell me the answer going forward.
Yeah.  I mean, you did point to the two years of liability from the day you decide this case and all of that overhang, but to answer your specific question  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, this statutory language, you know, it is relatively clear. And you might have been -- be -- be charged with having read it.  And going forward, you have two very simple solutions.  One is to get consent.  Easy enough.  People do it every day.  And the other is to stop selling people's private information.  Take your pick.
Yeah.  Or put everything behind a pay wall.  That would be great.  But I guess what I would say is that --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Not the same thing.
Well, I think that's one way that people will try to deal with this. But, as to the question  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Can you answer --
-- of whether consent is easy, the  --the statute's set up --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But what's the problem with not?
I'm sorry?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What's the problem with not disclosing private video view?
Oh, that  --that is --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean, it -- it's a business for you, and it might end your business if you don't want to get consent, but  if you want to stay in the business, get consent, or just don't do it.  What -- other than that you have created a business model that might contradict the law, because we still have a lot of open issues, what's the problem?

So, I mean, the -- the problem is the pay wall issue, which is the reason that material is available for "free" on the Internet is precisely because it's being financed by targeted advertisement.  And  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So people will be told that if you want to see this, you have to give consent.
Right.  And  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And so they'll make the choice of whether they want to watch it for free and have their view -- their viewing sold to other people or they won't.  I mean, it'll be up to the person, which seems to  me the way it should be.

So I guess what I would say to try to answer the question, I'm just not sure the consent is going to be easy as you imagine.  Certainly, Congress tried to make  consent relatively sort of sticky and said that it had to be in a separate -- a separate formulation.  It couldn't be with when you get consent to anything else.  And, certainly, the way these cases have been litigated, people  have argued that the consent, even when websites have tried to get consent, wasn't clear enough, wasn't unmistakable.  That could get  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, that'll always be the argument.  But it seems, just technologically, isn't it pretty easy for  -- for you all to obtain consent going forward? It'll be a little more hassle for all of us, but  --
For everyone.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.  But one  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's just one of those cookies boxes that comes up, right?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Wouldn't you do it the exact same way?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I mean, we do that a thousand times a day.

I know you do that a thousand times a day.  I will say that Congress, when it was -- when it was setting up this statute, did try to provide the consent, informed written consent.  It also said that it has to be provided in a clear and conspicuous manner for the consumer to withdraw on a case-by-case basis. So I  -- I -- I think, look, I'm not telling you that it's impossible, but I don't think you should decide this case about the meaning of "consumer" on the assumption that consent is absolutely easy.  And I do think what they would do, because they don't know who's a consumer  because they don't know who bought a chicken sandwich or who bought a dog bandana, they're going to ask consent from everybody.  And right there is a signal that something's off because  the statute requires consent from the consumer to the disclosure of the consumer's information.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, the definition might have been under-inclusive back in the day given modern technology, the definition of "consumer."  I mean, maybe the  -- the real concern Congress had if you translate it to today would be everyone who views the video.

I don't know that that's the case.  I mean, I think that's, you know, open to speculation.  But, as we point out in the brief, I think the one thing that's not open to speculation is that if Congress passes a statute to address the issues with targeted advertisement, they're not going to have  coverage turn on the happenstance of where you bought a chicken sandwich or where you bought a dog bandana.  I mean, that's kind of lunacy.  And that's why I think when you get to that kind of result you go back.  And then, to the point of  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But, Mr. Clement, take this  --the -- the -- the facts of this case, right?  So I  --I don't know 247, but there's a sports site and somebody gets a newsletter,  purchases a newsletter from that site.
It was a free newsletter, so they don't purchase it.  It's free.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Just let's assume that they  --
Just the way you sign up for, like, The New York Times.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- they purchase something from that site.
Yep.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then they watch a lot of videos.  And let's say a judge does  this.  And then it turns out that the judge watches some pretty funky sports videos, you know, like a lot of women wrestling or something.  (Laughter.)

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And that's embarrassing.  That's embarrassing and exactly  the way Congress thought we're passing this statute to prevent disclosure of that information.  So why is it like this case?  It kind of falls  -- you know, a lot of times we get cases that they don't fall within the heartland  of the statute, and we say, oh, well, the heartland of the statute isn't the whole statute.  The paradigmatic case isn't the only case.  But couldn't this case kind of be the paradigmatic case?  It's like you can, like, watch lots of embarrassing sports videos that  you don't want anybody else to know about.  A judge could.

I mean, I think it's hard to watch a lot of embarrassing videos on 247Sports based on my perusal of it.  But, like, you know, I don't know, maybe, like,  watching, you know, Chicago Bears films is embarrassing in certain parts of the country.  I don't know.  Maybe it is embarrassing.  The point is, though, it shouldn't turn on whether you also subscribed to a free  online newsletter, a free email newsletter. See, the  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Maybe that's right. Maybe that's right.  Maybe the thing that  Congress should do as they look at this again is to take away that limitation.  But  -- but -- but that wouldn't really serve your purpose, would it?  I mean, that's  -- that's a limitation that works in your favor, and the fact that it  excludes some people who might be embarrassed doesn't seem like an argument for your interpretation of the statute.

Well, here's what I think is an argument for my statute, which is it's undeniable that the statute turns on that happenstance, whether you get the chicken sandwich, whether you subscribe to the free  email newsletter, and that doesn't make a lot of sense.  And then the other thing that doesn't make a lot of sense is, because they've untethered the "consumer" definition from  "personally identifying information" and from "video tape service provider," then you get the situation where there's no temporal connection whatsoever.  So, under their theory, I can buy my chicken sandwich 10 years ago, I can buy my recliner 15 years ago, and then I don't watch a video on the website until a decade later.  Congress would never write a statute like that.  If they really expected people to be able to -- and I'll say it again -- mix and match consumer status with personal information  and video watching, they would have put some temporal limit that connected the two.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Clement --
And then  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- doesn't yours have a problem with temporal limit too, though? May  -- may -- let me just make sure I understand your theory.
Yeah.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If said judge purchases a subscription to 247Sports that allows, you know, him or her to watch these videos at Point A and then five or 10 years later watches a free video from 247Sports, I mean, haven't you also created a temporal  -- there's a gap?

So there could be a gap in certain situations, but I think it's a very, like, narrow gap.  I don't think you're going  to have millions of consumers that are all of a sudden VPPA consumers.  But it's also -- there is no gap in this sense.  If the initial purchase is a video purchase or, I think, to be more precise, is a prerecorded video cassette tape or similar audiovisual material, there is, under the statute, an immediate opportunity to give advance consent for two years.  And so that provision that was added in 2013, even in the somewhat funky hypo I think you're giving me, I mean, that  -- that advance consent provision works sensibly from the get-go, whereas, under my friend's position, you could buy a dog bandana and then you could give advance consent to the disclosure of PII before there's any PII under his reading of the statute, and then five years later, when you finally have PII, your advance consent has already expired.  And that just shows, like, every provision in this statute is  --makes sense if you tether what makes you a consumer to what  generates PII in the first instance.  And --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States
