text_blocks.text: Except, Mr. -- Mr. Clement, I still think you -- you have a line-drawing problem because, from the standpoint of the statute being concerned about the disclosure of personally identifying  information, you are creating two different categories of customers.  You're creating two  different categories of people.  In other words, the statute only protects those whose personally identifying information is disclosed if they have a consumer relationship that involves buying  those videos, as opposed to those who have their personally identifying information disclosed, but they bought something else.  I think that's irrational as well if the thrust and the point of the statute is to protect the -- against the disclosure of personally identifying information.  And I understand your point being that because we have any definition of "consumer," it's under-inclusive.  You have people who are not consumers whose personally identifying information might be disclosed.  Justice Kagan  brought that point up with you.  But, fine, assuming we have that oddity, you seem to be making yet another one by carving up even more the category of people whose personally identifying information is disclosed.

I don't think I'm carving it up more, and I think I'm doing exactly what Congress intended.  And Congress  --you know, for those who read Senate reports, Congress focused on this possibility that you could have the department store and they would sell a couple of video tapes and they would sell a lot of  --bunch of other stuff, and they didn't think they wanted to protect the other goods and services.  Now my friend will tell you, yeah, that piece of legislative history focused on the PII definition.  But here's the thing:  It would be pretty weird to have the thing in the  statute that does the limiting work to be a definition that by its terms is expressly inclusive.  That's not a well-designed tool to do limiting work.  What is a well  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I guess I don't understand -- I don't understand your answer to my question.  I mean, I'm saying that what  mattered in the statute was the unlawful disclosure without consent of personally identifying information.  And your interpretation of the statute has that coming out differently, the same set of circumstances happening, coming out differently depending upon what particular item the consumer purchased.  And I don't understand  why that should be the dividing line or why that makes any sense in this concept.

So, to me, it makes a ton of sense because what makes you a consumer is a transaction that generates personal identifiable information.  And when you buy a book or a dog bandana, under both parties' view of the statute, that doesn't generate any personally identifiable  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But that's not what makes you a consumer under the statute, right? The statute has a different category of personally identifying information than it does of consumer.  So it doesn't make you a consumer  to have personally identifying information under this statute.

What I'm saying is, if there is a close connection between what makes you a consumer and what generates personally identifiable information, the whole statute, including the consent provisions, work coherently.  And that's why I think Congress said that when you buy a video, you're a consumer, but when you buy a book or you buy gasoline or you buy a chicken sandwich, you're not a consumer because, at the moment you buy the book, the  --the chicken sandwich, the gasoline, there's no personally identifiable information.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right.
So you don't really --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The statute doesn't say that.  That's your theory of what the  statute said when it said "goods or services."

It's both parties' agreed understanding of personally identifiable information until you get specific video information.  And speaking of specific video information -- I don't want to sit down before  I make this point -- my friend tries to make something of the fact that the word "video" appears in the personally identifiable  information definition before the phrase "from a video tape service provider."  And he says, aha, they know how to use it.  But he ignores that they use two words.  They didn't use "video."  They used "specific video."  And there's a very good  reason they did that because there's another provision in the statute, (b)(2)(D), that allows the disclosure of general subject matter information about videos in certain circumstances.  So "specific video" is doing  work in the "personal identifiable information" definition that there's no analogue to in the definition of "consumer."  And here's something else to consider. If you did what my friend wants you to do to  make this an easier case, if Congress had put "video" in front of "goods or services," it would have gone a long way to making the phrase  "from a video tape service provider" redundant. And my friend tells you we try to avoid redundancy if at all possible.  But think of the way the statute works.  In order to be a consumer, you have to rent, buy, or subscribe to a video.  And if  -- no matter what else your business does, if you rent, sell, or deliver videos, prerecorded videos, you are per force a video tape service provider.  So, if you had a hypothetical statute that has the word that he wants in it, it said video goods and services from a video tape  service provider, at that point, you have two options.  Either you admit that "from a video tape service provider" is doing no work, or you do what you might do, which is to struggle to give it some meaning, you would say, ah, you know, there actually are some video goods or services that aren't actually prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.  So take, for example, a blank VCR tape.  Now that's clearly a video good or  service, but it's not prerecorded and it doesn't involve any personal identifiable information.  So, in a hypothetical statute  that had the word "video" where my friend wants it, you probably would look to "from a video tape service provider" to limit the scope of -- of video goods or services.  But, if you can look to "from a video tape service provider" to limit the scope of video goods or services, I don't know why you can't look to it to limit the scope of goods or services.  And I do think that is natural, ordinary meaning, as Justice Alito alluded to, but it also makes particular sense in a statute that's focused on privacy concerns that uniquely arise out of video transactions.  Go back to the example I started with with goods or services from a medical service provider.  Okay.  In ordinary English, I don't  think that covers buying a cup of coffee from the hospital.  But, in a medical privacy statute, nobody cares whether I got, like, you know, half caf, but what they care about is whether I had an appendectomy or I had plastic  surgery or something.  So you would naturally in that context say that a consumer of goods or services from a medical service provider talks about people that got actual medical services, not people who got a valet parking service when they got to the -- the medical office. And that's what we're asking to you do here.  And my friend's whole position really  depends on reading three words in the definition in isolation.  But it's a 15 -word definition, and the other 12 words all direct  you to audiovisual materials that are similar to prerecorded video cassettes because it starts with this triad of terms:  Renter, buyer, or subscriber. Weird.  It doesn't appear anywhere else in the U.S. Code, but it precisely captures the three ways that you got video tapes in 1988, and it starts with rental, which was the  --was the single most obvious way you would get video tapes in 1988.  And then, if you carry through to the definition of a video tape service provider, you see the same triad.  You see selling video  tapes, renting video tapes, or delivering them. And it all works together as a harmonious whole.  And I wouldn't just interpret those three words in splendid isolation and read them  to the limits of the world.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, you argue and your amici argue that accepting the  Petitioner's interpretation of (a)(1) would lead to drastic consequences, and, in response  to that, it is said that's not necessarily so because you could win under other provisions of this statute. And, of course, you don't want to say no, we stand a chance of losing under these other provisions based on the same sort of linguistic interpretation that Petitioner is advancing here.  And, therefore, I think, for this reason, Mr. Hammack was asked about (a)(4). And I wonder if you could say something about (a)(4) and what you understand the statute to  mean when it talks about "any person engaged in the business of delivery of audiovisual materials that are similar to video cassette tapes"?  What does it mean to be "in the business"?  And does it mean  --does it reach any  -- any person or entity that derives any economic benefit from providing access to  videos or, at the other extreme, does it mean any person or entity that is engaged solely in that or predominantly in that?  What does it mean?

So I don't think it can mean, unfortunately  -- it would help me win this case eventually  --if I thought it meant, like, predominantly or exclusively.  But I think that's pretty impossible to square with the idea that Congress plainly wanted to capture department stores that sold videos back  in 1988, grocery stores that sold videos in 1988.  So I think that if you're engaged in the business, and, you know, there's a reference to interstate or foreign commerce, so I'm thinking they're casting a pretty wide net,  and you deliver videos, it seems most naturally read  --and some of you are maybe suggesting I'm most  -- not most naturally reading "consumer," but I actually think I'm most naturally reading all 15 words.  But I think, most naturally read, this would capture Chick-fil-A, La-Z-Boy, all of these things, because they're certainly in business and they are delivering videos.  Now, like, I don't want to put two feet on that because I could be back in some court arguing no, no, no, that, you know, it means something slightly different.  But I think it's tough given that Congress clearly  wanted to capture the  -- the --the -- the department stores and the grocery stores. And that's why I really think the most natural way to narrow this statute is to get the definition of "consumer" right and limit it to the consumers -- and, again, we're -- we're talking about the (a)(4) definition.  But the  (a)(4) definition's kind of baked right in to the definition of "consumer."  And that's why I think it would have been redundant if  -- I mean, you know, just to make the redundancy point one more time, I mean, (a)(4) is already baked in and already  says a prerecorded video cassette tape or similar audiovisual material.  So I suppose what Congress could have said in the definition of "consumer" is consumer means any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials from a video  tape service provider, which, of course, is a provider of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right, right.  Yeah.

But that would be hopelessly awkward and redundant.  And it -- it just underscores that if Congress had done both, it would have been redundant, and I think there was a perfectly good reason it left "goods or services" unmodified.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, the statute means what the statute means regardless of the  -- of the consequences, but it would be interesting to know whether "in the business of" means deriving any sort of commercial advantage from providing access to videos on a  website because that would seem to impose huge retroactive liability on a broad, broad range of entities.  And I'm not sure I understood Mr. Hammack's definition of what it means to be "in the business of."  Maybe he'll take another  shot at that on -- on rebuttal.

Yeah.  I  --I must confess I did not understand it either.  And I don't think it explains away Chick-fil-A.  And just to put it in concrete terms, if you look at the complaint in this case, he alleges that there are over a hundred thousand subscribers  to 247Sports.com  that he wants to represent in a class action.  Now I'm not great at math, but $2500 per plaintiff in a class action that includes at least a hundred thousand people, I think, is $250 million of liability in this case alone.  And then you look at the Chamber brief and all those footnotes, you look at The Retail Litigation Center appendix and all of those cases, and there's a reason, I think, as you alluded to, that every district court judge that looks at this thinks this cannot be right, this is crazy.  And I would suggest that a careful textual reading of all 15 words in this definition actually gets you to the result that, yes, it's not right.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Sotomayor?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, some very intelligent circuit court judges have disagreed  with you.  The linchpin of your argument is that the transaction that some -- that makes someone a VPPA consumer must be the same one that generates PII.  But the VPPA refutes that.  "(D) governs the use of personally identifiable information"  -- I'm quoting -- "obtained in any manner as evidence in some governmental proceeding."  So you don't have to be a consumer in there.  And it requires destroying such information as soon as practicable.  Those provisions apply regardless of whether the  information concerns a consumer.  So, if the statute explicitly envisions that PII can exist without a  consumer, I don't understand why it's absurd that a consumer might exist who hasn't yet  generated but will generate PII because you're only liable if you are disclosing PII of someone's video -viewing. So what's  --I don't understand.
So I do think there is a fundamental difference between having PII without a consumer and having a consumer that has no PII.  Now, as we point out in our brief --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, no, a consumer will have PII because you're going to disclose PII.  You're only liable --
No, no --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- whether -- what you're saying that it's different than if the consumer doesn't create it at that moment of the transaction.

No, what I'm saying is, actually, under his view as I understand it, if you go into the Blockbuster, the last one, the brick-and-mortar store, you buy your dog bandana, and then you never look at the Blockbuster website, then you are a consumer in  his view, but you have no PII.  You are an inchoate VPPA consumer.  And I think that is far more anomalous than  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  Then why?  When you finally buy something, it is what you buy, that video-viewing, that's being protected.

Well, you don't have to buy anything.  And that's another anomaly. See, under the statute Congress wrote, if you  walked in to a  --even a video store and they gave you a video, you're not protected by the statute.  You have to have a video transaction.  And what makes his position and I would -- I would respectfully suggest consumers without PII so anomalous is they essentially make this free online viewing of videos that  otherwise doesn't make anybody a consumer and then they retroactively become a consumer because they bought a chicken sandwich 10 years later, they look -- they subscribed to the  local newspaper, they signed up for a free email.  I don't think that makes any sense. And I do think it does damage to the statute that having the converse doesn't because, as  I've alluded to, all of the consent provisions are premised on the idea that the person that can provide consent is the consumer.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kagan?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I just want to make sure I understand your view of (a)(3).  So this is the PII includes information which identifies a person as having requested or  obtained specific video materials.  What does "includes" mean, do you believe?
So I think that it means something different from "means."  I think it does set a floor.  And that's why I don't think the definition of PII can do the limiting  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, what kind of floor are you saying?  In other words, does it include information which identifies a person  as having requested or obtained other materials or services?  I mean, your bandanas or your La-Z-Boys, do you think that there's no requirement that the person have requested or  obtained video materials or services?
Well, it's tricky, right, because, if we're going to be literal, I mean, "includes" --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, I want to  --I want to know what you -- you think.
So --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Does it include bandanas and La -Z-Boys?

So I would say that it doesn't.  But it's hard to get there from a literal reading of the text because the textual definition is just an "includes" definition.  Now I know from the Senate report, which I read, that Congress didn't want to protect private information about dog bandanas or furniture that you bought from a department store.  So, if we're going to be faithful to the intent that was reflected in the Senate report, we have to figure some way to limit this statute so that it protects video information and not bandana information.  And I would respectfully suggest that, you know, you could do it, and I -- I would suppose I might even argue for it someday, but  it's hard to get the limit from a definition that's an inclusive definition.  And I think  the better place to get the limiting principle is from the definition of "consumer."

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Gorsuch?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Do you disagree with the American Newspaper amicus brief that "similar" would at least require content like full-length movies and television shows that were on video tape lining Blockbuster shelves?
Ultimately, when that issue comes up, I would  -- you know, in that --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You're going to -- you're going to take that position?
I am going to take that position.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You'd agree with newspapers that that  --that that  -- that -- that is a distinction?
And I might even go one further and agree with Judge Randolph that they have to be --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Physical?
-- physical.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.
Because, you know, materials is kind of physical.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.  Thank you.
So, if you -- yeah.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kavanaugh?  Justice Barrett?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Do you concede that Salazar has standing?

We haven't argued that he doesn't.  And I guess this is what  --if I could -- I think the best answer to that is I  think it depends on what you make of page 11 of the Meta brief.  I don't know if you have it in front of you, but it's -- you know, it's got this gobbledegook.  And that's  -- that's what's disclosed to a third party.  And so I take it the question would be, is the disclosure of gobbledegook to a third party sufficiently close to the common law analogue of disclosing personal information to a third party to satisfy Article III?  That's a tricky question.  I mean, if you want us to, we can brief it.  I would really hate for the Court to reject  -- like, it  -- to say that there's definitively standing here in this case without any briefing.  So I  don't know if you can drop a footnote and say this is just a drive-by jurisdictional ruling -- (Laughter.)
--so you can ignore it in the future.  I don't know if you're allowed to do that, but  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You raised it in the district court.
We did raise it in the district court.  And then we --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But then dropped it before the Sixth Circuit.
We did.  But you know the funny thing about standing arguments, you can't really drop them.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right.

So, if you -- if you're intrigued by that question, you know, I'd be happy to provide supplemental briefing.  And  -- but I -- but I do think the question really comes down to whether that gobbledegook is  sufficiently close to a common law analogue.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, this gobbledegook also presents the question of whether it's PII, right, if nobody can look at it and really identify -- only a computer can figure out what this means?

Yeah, and maybe that's one more reason to not decide the standing question definitively without more briefing  because I do think there is a close relationship between the standing question and the PII question.  So, you know, if you say there's standing here because it's sort of not really totally gobbledegook, then my friend's going to try to use that in the lower courts to say, aha, it is personally identifiable information.  So, again, I'm  --we're happy to brief it if you'd like us to.  But I  -- I do think it would be a mistake to definitively decide  standing without any briefing.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Jackson?  Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, Mr. Hammack?

Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice.  Just a couple of points.  First, I think it's really important to keep our eye on the ball that what we're looking for here in Section (b)(1) is any consumer of such provider, any consumer.  So, when we  -- when we have questions about, well, what about someone  who purchased a dog bandana or someone who purchased a La-Z-Boy recliner or someone who purchased something or rented something years ago, our question is made simpler by the fact that (b)(1) says any consumer of such provider. So is someone who rented something a number of years ago or purchases a chicken sandwich from a provider, is that person any consumer of such provider?  The answer has to be yes.  That's the most natural reading.  It  aligns with ordinary meaning all over the statute.  Second, I want to address the -- the point that my friend on the other side made  regarding this shift in the number of cases brought happening, you know, a decade or so ago.  And that shift did not occur because  plaintiffs suddenly woke up one day and discovered the Video Privacy Protection Act.  It occurred because of the advent of pixel technology, this technology that all kinds of  businesses started embedding in their websites that is automatically target  --tracking and disclosing all sorts of personally identifiable  information about you, including the personally identifiable information specifically defined in this statute.  Third, that huge liability problem, if we get through all of the various elements of  the statute and land in a world where there is large liability, I won't dispute that that's a possibility, but I think it's -- it reflects necessarily the fact that this is a huge scale disclosure regime.  That large liability is  only possible because of the scope of the disclosures of personally identifiable information here.  Fourth, I want to address the mix-or-match point that my friend on the other side made.  And I would say it's entirely  unsurprising that you might mix or match as between what makes you a consumer and what gives rise to PII.  That's exactly why and the  direct result of the fact that Congress mentioned two different relationships to two different subject matters from the same source across those two provisions.  It's the inevitable consequence of that.  To go to Justice Jackson's point regarding the  --the hypothetical that you were discussing with my friend on the other side, I think that exchange really shows the incredible  loophole that their reading creates where they can basically structure themselves around VPPA compliance by making sure that you request or obtain video materials or services, but we've structured our business so that you never  actually rent, purchase, or subscribe to them. You'll rent, purchase, and subscribe to lots of other things but not those video materials.  So, suddenly, we can disclose your personally identifiable information with impunity without your consent.  That, I think, should be the  anomaly when you're looking at this statute.  Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  The case is submitted.
